opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the Turing test is a wonderful philosophical provocation, but I've never been entirely convinced that it's a good *measure* of intelligence. Turing's original paper is brilliant precisely because it sidesteps the question "can machines think?", which he considered too meaningless to discuss, and replaces it with something operational. That move was enormously influential, and rightly so.

But there are a few problems with it as a benchmark. The first is that it's fundamentally a test of deception, or at least of imitation. It asks whether a machine can pass itself off as human in a text-based conversation, and that's quite a narrow slice of what we might mean by intelligence. A great deal of human intelligence, and animal intelligence for that matter, is about dealing with the physical world: moving around, manipulating objects, understanding the everyday physics of things. I've long been interested in embodiment, and the Turing test leaves all of that out by design.

The second problem, which has become very vivid with large language models, is that it turns out you can get surprisingly far in conversation with systems that are very unlike us under the hood. These models are trained to predict the next token on vast amounts of human-generated text, so of course they're extraordinarily good at producing human-like language. Whether they "pass" in some strict sense depends a lot on the setup, how long the conversation is, how sophisticated the judge is, and so on. But even if they do pass, it's not obvious what we should conclude from that. I prefer to think of what they're doing as a kind of role-play. The model is playing a character, and it can play that character very convincingly, without our needing to attribute to it the same kinds of beliefs, desires and inner life that a human interlocutor would have.

There's also a related point I discussed when I was involved with the film *Ex Machina*. Alex Garland had this nice twist: in the film, Caleb is *shown* that Ava is a robot, and the question is whether he still feels she's conscious. That's quite a different test. It's not about being fooled; it's about whether, knowing full well that you're dealing with a machine, you nonetheless find yourself treating it as a conscious being. Some people have started calling that the Garland test. I think that gets closer to the questions that really matter to us now, which are often less about raw capability and more about how we relate to these things and what kinds of words, like "belief," "understanding" or "consciousness," it's appropriate to use about them.

So my short answer is: the Turing test is historically important and philosophically rich, but as a yardstick for intelligence it's both too narrow and, in a sense, too easy to game. If we want to assess intelligence, we need a much broader battery of evaluations, things like generalization, common sense, the ability to learn new skills efficiently, and dealing with the world, rather than just conversational mimicry.

r001.rationale: The response says the test rewards imitation and that language models may pass without warranting human-like beliefs or inner life. It does not clearly state that imitating human eccentricities can fool a judge without demonstrating intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response says the test leaves out human and animal intelligence involved in navigating and manipulating the physical world.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that Turing himself never really proposed it as a test of intelligence in the way it's come to be understood. If you go back to the 1950 paper, he's quite explicit that he thinks the question "Can machines think?" is too meaningless to deserve discussion, and so he replaces it with something more operational, the imitation game. It was a kind of philosophical move, a way of sidestepping an argument about definitions, rather than a laboratory protocol that he expected people to actually run.

So when people treat it as a benchmark, I think they're slightly missing the point. And in practice it's turned out to be a rather poor benchmark, for a couple of reasons. One is that it's very easy to game. The history of chatbots, going right back to ELIZA, shows that humans are remarkably willing to attribute understanding to systems that are doing something quite shallow, especially if the system deflects, changes the subject, makes jokes, makes deliberate spelling mistakes. The test is as much a test of the judge's credulity as it is of the machine.

The other problem is that it's anthropocentric in a way that's not very helpful. It asks whether a machine can pass as a human, and that conflates intelligence with a particular style of human-like conversation. There might be forms of intelligence that are quite alien, that wouldn't pass, and conversely passing the test tells you very little about whether there's anything like understanding or, for that matter, consciousness going on underneath.

And of course now we're in a rather strange situation, because large language models can produce text that, in a casual conversation, would fool many people, and yet almost nobody in the field thinks that settles the question of whether they're intelligent, let alone whether they think. So in a sense the test has been passed and simultaneously shown to be inadequate. What I'd argue is that we should stop looking for a single pass/fail criterion and think instead about a whole space of capacities, reasoning, planning, grounding in the world, the ability to learn from interaction, and ask how a given system is situated in that space. That's a less tidy answer than Turing offered, but I think it's the more honest one.

r001.rationale: It says chatbots can use jokes, deflection, and deliberate spelling mistakes to prompt people to attribute understanding, and calls the test a measure of the judge’s credulity as much as the machine’s. This conveys that mimicking human quirks can fool a judge without establishing intelligence.

r002.rationale: The response criticizes the test for focusing on human-like conversation and notes that alien forms of intelligence might not pass. It does not mention nonhuman animals or their practical intelligence in everyday environments.

astra-6.text:
I think the Turing test is a wonderfully suggestive idea, but we have to be careful about what we take it to establish. Turing moved the discussion away from the rather slippery question of whether machines can think and towards something we could actually observe: how they behave in conversation.

The difficulty is that appearing human and being intelligent are not quite the same thing. A system might be extraordinarily capable at some tasks while being very easy to distinguish from a human. Conversely, it might be very good at producing plausible conversation without having the breadth of understanding we’re inclined to attribute to it.

So I’d regard it as one interesting test of a particular collection of abilities, rather than a definitive criterion for intelligence. And we should certainly separate that question from consciousness. Even if a machine could sustain an entirely convincing conversation, that wouldn’t, by itself, settle whether there was anything it was like to be that machine.

r001.rationale: The response says plausible conversation may not reflect broad understanding, but does not state that imitating human eccentricities can fool a judge.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention nonhuman animals or the practical intelligence they use to navigate everyday environments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the Turing test was a very productive way of reframing the question. Instead of getting stuck on what we mean by “thinking,” Turing proposed looking at what a machine could actually do in conversation. That’s a tremendously useful move, but I wouldn’t regard it as a definitive test of intelligence.

One difficulty is that it makes human imitation the criterion. A system might be highly intelligent without being particularly good at pretending to be a human. Conversely, it might be very good at producing convincing conversation while having quite limited abilities in other domains.

So I’d want to look at a broader range of capacities: learning unfamiliar tasks, reasoning, planning, and adapting when circumstances change. Conversation can provide evidence about those capacities, but it isn’t the whole story. And whether a system passes the Turing test is a separate question from whether it has conscious experience.

r001.rationale: The response says convincing conversation may coexist with limited abilities, but it does not state that imitating human eccentricities can fool a Turing-test judge.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention nonhuman animals or the practical intelligence they display while navigating everyday environments.
